Carousel outline: The MRI export stack before CAM math

Slide 1: Do not start with the cap formula
- Start with the files.

Slide 2: Recovery Reconciliation
- Tenant recovery result by pool, in detail mode.

Slide 3: GL Transaction Detail
- Account, date, source, reference, and amount.

Slide 4: Rent Roll
- Tenant ID, suite, rentable SF, and lease dates.

Slide 5: Tenant Billing History
- Use it when estimate charges or invoice history are the question.

Slide 6: The period check
- Decide whether period 13 or 14 belongs in the year.

Slide 7: The entity check
- Make sure the expense entity and property selection match.

Slide 8: The order
- Export stack first. Lease math second.

The first 30 days after a tenant audit notice are mostly about control.

Who owns the response?
Which lease clause governs the request?
Which years are in scope?
Which records can be produced without scrambling?
Which disputed items are math errors, ambiguous lease reads, or unsupported claims?

That sorting work matters because a blanket denial is rarely useful.

A stronger response says:

This item is conceded.
This item is supported by these records.
This item depends on this lease interpretation.
This item is outside the documented scope.

CapVeri helps build that trail before the notice arrives, so the response starts from files and calculations instead of memory.

90% and 95% are not interchangeable gross-up targets.

On $500,000 of variable expenses at 70% occupancy:

Gross-up to 90%:
$500,000 / 0.70 x 0.90 = $642,857

Gross-up to 95%:
$500,000 / 0.70 x 0.95 = $678,571

Difference:
$35,714 in the variable expense pool.

The spreadsheet may treat that as one input cell.

The lease treats it as the rule.

CapVeri keeps the target tied to the lease clause because a clean formula with the wrong threshold is still the wrong calculation.

Move-outs make annual pro-rata math easy to get wrong.

A tenant that leaves on June 30 should not be treated like a full-year tenant.

A tenant that expands on July 1 should not have one annual numerator.

The year needs to be split into the periods the lease actually occupied:

Before move-out.
After move-out.
Before expansion.
After expansion.

Then the share gets calculated for each period and prorated by lease days.

CapVeri handles that as date-bound math, not a year-end shortcut.

Because the rent roll snapshot is a starting point, not the whole story.

One CAM cap error stays quiet until expenses spike:

Compounding from last year's actual bill instead of last year's cap ceiling.

If actuals were below the ceiling, the two bases separate.

Year after year, the incorrect ceiling drifts lower. In a calm expense year, the issue may stay hidden because actuals are still under both numbers.

Then insurance, security, or maintenance jumps.

Suddenly the cap binds, and the building is using a ceiling that was quietly underbuilt for years.

CapVeri tracks the cap path from the prior ceiling, not from whatever happened to be billed last year.

That distinction is dull until it matters.

Then it is the whole calculation.

Carousel outline: The admin fee circularity problem

Slide 1: "15% of CAM" may not be enough
- The base decides the fee.

Slide 2: Net method
- Fee = rate x expense base.

Slide 3: Gross method
- Fee is included in the total that the fee is based on.

Slide 4: The circularity
- The fee depends on a number that includes the fee.

Slide 5: The algebraic fix
- Fee = rate x base / (1 - rate).

Slide 6: The capped method
- Calculate the fee, then apply the lease ceiling.

Slide 7: The audit packet
- Keep the lease clause and worksheet together.

Slide 8: The control
- Method first. Percentage second.

The BOMA 2024 rollout step worth protecting:

Run the reconciliation both ways before go-live.

Current measurement.
Updated measurement.
Tenant by tenant comparison.
Variance review.
System check.

That parallel run catches the quiet mistakes:

Building total updated, suite RSF not updated.
Pro-rata shares no longer sum correctly.
Gross-up denominator still uses the old rentable area.
One lease references a fixed BOMA version while another allows updates.

CapVeri treats BOMA 2024 as an input-control project, not a slogan.

The first live statement should not be the first test.

CapVeri can find CAM risk without becoming the accounting system.

The useful data is already there:

Recovery report.
GL detail.
Rent roll.
Billing history when needed.

The question is whether those exports are complete, flat, tied to the same period, and matched back to lease rules.

That is the export-first view of CAM reconciliation.

No direct ERP integration promise.
No "rip out the system" story.
No black-box math.

Just the files property teams already know, tested against deterministic lease calculations.

Sometimes the fastest path to control is not a deeper integration.

It is a cleaner export.

The useful question after a tenant flags a CAM charge is:

What happens next?

Not "who made the mistake?"
Not "can we explain this away?"

What happens next?

If the GL supports it, produce the invoice and clause.

If the math is wrong, recalculate and document the correction.

If the lease language is ambiguous, separate the interpretation issue from the arithmetic.

If the request is outside scope, say why with the lease language attached.

CapVeri is built for that response path: source record, lease rule, calculation, review status.

That is a better posture than searching through old folders while the clock is already running.

The safest place for AI in CAM reconciliation is before the math, not inside it.

Use it to extract lease clauses.
Use it to identify likely expense categories.
Use it to surface the fields a human needs to verify.

Then stop.

The calculation should run on confirmed inputs and explicit formulas.

That split matters because extraction can be reviewed. Math has to be reproducible.

CapVeri keeps AI-assisted document work separate from deterministic calculation for exactly that reason.

No model should be asked to "probably" allocate a tenant's charge.

The ledger should show the work.

When the question is "what did we bill?" the GL is not enough.

For Yardi teams, Charge Schedule often becomes the support file.

It helps answer:

Which estimate charge was billed?
When did the estimate change?
Did the billed side move when the budget changed?
Which charge code carried the amount?

That matters because reconciliation is two-sided:

Adjusted actual obligation.
Estimated billings already collected.

The tenant's balance sits between those numbers.

CapVeri keeps billing support tied to the reconciliation because a correct expense pool still needs a correct credit for what was already paid.

Carousel outline: A recovery gap is not one thing

Slide 1: Low recovery is a question
- Not a conclusion.

Slide 2: GL mapping gap
- Expense exists, but the recovery pool did not pick it up.

Slide 3: Gross-up gap
- Variable expenses were not normalized below the lease threshold.

Slide 4: Cap constraint
- The lease may limit what can be billed.

Slide 5: Classification noise
- Recoverable, excluded, capital, and landlord-only costs got mixed.

Slide 6: Denominator drift
- Tenant shares changed because the denominator moved.

Slide 7: The useful output
- A reason code, not a vague leakage number.

Slide 8: The CapVeri view
- Model the gap before calling it recoverable.

Each material CAM statement line should have a lineage.

Not a paragraph of explanation.

A lineage:

GL account.
Invoice support.
Lease treatment.
Gross-up status.
Cap status.
Tenant share.
Estimate credit.

When that chain is visible, review gets calmer.

When it is missing, a simple tenant question can turn into a reconstruction project.

CapVeri pushes for source-linked statements because CAM confidence is not created by the final PDF. It is created by the records behind it.

The statement is the output.

The lineage is the control.

Gross-up has a stop sign.

If the lease target is 95% and the building is already at or above 95%, the gross-up factor should not inflate the variable pool.

That sounds obvious.

It still needs to be checked, because a spreadsheet can apply the formula mechanically:

Target occupancy / actual occupancy.

Without the threshold guard, the calculation can move when it should stay at actuals.

CapVeri treats gross-up as a rule set, not just a formula:

Only variable expenses.
Only when the lease allows it.
Only to the lease-defined target.
No inflation above the target condition.

Small guardrails help catch expensive-looking mistakes before they harden into the packet.

The reconciliation question is not only:

What did the property spend?

It is also:

What did the tenant already pay?

A strong true-up needs both sides:

Adjusted expense pool.
Lease-defined pro-rata share.
Any allowed gross-up or cap logic.
Estimated billings collected during the year.
Final balance due or credit.

Miss the estimate credit, and the statement can be wrong even if the expense math is right.

CapVeri ties billing history back into the calculation because reconciliation is not a GL report.

It is a settlement.

The cleanest CAM review often starts with a file question:

Do the exports tie before anyone opens the workbook?

For Yardi teams, that means the Recovery Analysis, GL Analytics, and rent roll need the same property, the same reconciliation period, and detail-level output.

If one file is summary-level, the math may still look polished. The support will not.

That is where the control lives.

Export first. Tie the files. Then test the lease math.

What is the first export your team checks before statements go out?

Gross-up mistakes usually start before the formula.

The question is not just "what is the occupancy target?"

It is:

Which expenses are actually variable?

Property taxes do not become 95% occupied. Insurance does not become 95% occupied. A fixed management fee does not become 95% occupied.

Janitorial, utilities, trash, and similar usage-driven costs are the items that need the closer look.

The formula is only defensible after the pool is split.

If the split is wrong, the percentage will not rescue it.

Carousel outline: What belongs in the CAM audit packet?

Slide 1: The packet is the response
- A tenant audit request should not start a document hunt.

Slide 2: GL export
- Full year, property level, with account codes and descriptions.

Slide 3: Invoice index
- Vendor, date, amount, account, and a way to pull the backup fast.

Slide 4: Management fee calculation
- Base, rate, cap if any, and the lease clause used.

Slide 5: Pro-rata schedule
- Tenant RSF, denominator, percentage, and source for each number.

Slide 6: Gross-up workbook
- Occupancy, threshold, fixed-variable split, and normalized variable pool.

Slide 7: Cap bank schedule
- Base year, annual ceiling, actuals, unused capacity, and carry-forward balance.

Slide 8: The point
- Make the review traceable before the question arrives.

An MRI export can run clean and still miss the reconciliation answer.

One quiet reason: adjustment periods.

If period 13 or 14 belongs in the close process, a period 12 GL export can look complete while leaving year-end activity outside the file.

That is not a cap problem.

It is not a pro-rata problem.

It is an export boundary problem.

Before testing formulas, check entity, property, period range, and whether adjustment periods are intentionally included or intentionally excluded.

"We used the report" is not the same as "we exported the right accounting period."

Pro-rata share is a tiny percentage with a large blast radius.

The numerator gets attention because it is the tenant's space.

The denominator is where quiet drift shows up.

Leasable area and leased area are not interchangeable. If vacant suites fall out of the denominator, the occupied tenants carry a larger share of the same pool.

The expense did not change.

The allocation did.

Before sending a reconciliation, compare the denominator to the lease definition and the rent roll source behind it.

That one check can explain a lot of "why did my share move?" questions.

Cumulative caps need a ledger, not a memory.

The cap bank is easy to explain:

If actual controllable expenses are below the allowed ceiling, unused capacity may carry forward when the lease says the cap is cumulative.

The hard part is proving the balance later.

Each year needs the same basic row:

Base amount.
Annual cap ceiling.
Actual controllable amount.
Amount billed.
Unused capacity.
Bank balance.

When that schedule is missing, the next reconciliation starts with a trust problem.

If the lease says non-cumulative, the unused capacity disappears. If it says cumulative, the carry-forward needs to survive ownership changes, staff changes, and spreadsheet cleanups.

That is the control.

AI can help read documents.

CAM math needs a ledger.

The calculation has to answer ordinary questions:

Which lease clause controlled the pool?
Which expenses were included or excluded?
Which gross-up threshold was used?
Which denominator produced the tenant share?
Which cap ceiling limited the amount?

That is why CapVeri keeps extraction and calculation separate.

Extraction can be reviewed by a human.

The math runs through deterministic rules so the same inputs produce the same answer.

For financial work, "show the work" is not a nice-to-have.

It is the point.

Two admin fee calculations can use the same percentage and produce different answers.

That is why the first question is method, not rate.

Gross method: the fee is calculated on a pool that includes the fee.

Net method: the fee is calculated on the pool before the fee is added.

Capped method: the calculated fee is limited by a lease-defined ceiling.

The percentage is only half the instruction.

Before billing, document the base, the method, and the cap treatment if the lease has one.

A clean admin fee backup should be clear enough to audit.

BOMA 2024 is a measurement input, not a marketing badge.

For CAM, the practical question is simple:

Did the rentable square footage used in the reconciliation change?

If yes, the packet needs the source:

Old measurement.
New measurement.
Lease language that allows or blocks the update.
Effective date.
Tenant-level pro-rata impact.

CapVeri can work with BOMA-referenced measurement inputs.

That does not mean a certification, endorsement, or shortcut around the lease.

Measurement changes belong in the backup, not in someone's inbox after billing.

Treat recovery ratio like a smoke alarm.

When it drops, the answer is not automatically "bill more."

The first move is the comparison:

Recoverable operating expense pool.
Total CAM billed.
Difference by property.
Reason codes for the gap.

The reason codes matter more than the headline number.

A gap caused by a lease exclusion is not the same as a gap caused by an unmapped GL account.

A cap limitation is not the same as a missed gross-up.

The review should make the difference traceable enough for the team to decide what is recoverable, what is excluded, and what needs a setup fix.

Carousel outline: The Yardi export set before CAM review

Slide 1: Do not start with the spreadsheet
- Start with the export stack.

Slide 2: Recovery Analysis
- Tenant-level actuals, billings, variances, and recovery pools.

Slide 3: GL Analytics
- The transaction detail behind the recoverable expense pool.

Slide 4: Rent Roll with Lease Charges
- Tenant roster, rentable SF, lease timing, and charge setup.

Slide 5: Charge Schedule when needed
- Use it when the question is what was billed during the year.

Slide 6: The QA pass
- Same property, same period, detail mode, flat CSV.

Slide 7: The wrong order
- Debugging gross-up before the exports tie.

Slide 8: The right order
- Tie the files, then test the lease math.

The estimate letter is where expectations get set.

The reconciliation is where the actuals catch up.

If the estimate was stale all year, the true-up may be mathematically correct and still feel like a surprise.

That is why a mid-year check matters:

Current GL run rate.
Budget assumptions.
Vendor changes.
Insurance and tax movement.
Tenant estimate billings to date.

The goal is not to make the estimate perfect.

It is to catch obvious drift before it becomes the only thing the tenant remembers about the reconciliation.

Move-out reconciliations break when the year is treated as one flat period.

A tenant that leaves in May does not need the same date range as a tenant that stayed through December.

The control is simple:

Calculate the share.
Apply the correct expense pool.
Prorate by the lease days in the reconciliation period.
Tie the estimate billings already collected.

The mistake is skipping straight to the annual tenant percentage and hoping the timing works itself out.

It usually does not.

Partial-year occupancy needs its own row, not a footnote.

A useful CAM calculation should let a reviewer rerun the answer from the inputs.

That reviewer might be internal accounting.

It might be a CPA.

It might be the person who inherits the file two years from now.

Either way, the file needs more than a final number.

It needs:

The source export.
The lease rule.
The classification decision.
The formula.
The exact inputs.
The final tenant result.

CapVeri's math is built around that trace.

AI can help extract lease and document facts, but verified inputs and deterministic calculations are what make the result repeatable.

A tenant asks for CAM support.

What happens next inside the property team?

A. Someone sends the same packet by default.

B. Accounting pulls the GL while property management searches for invoices.

C. The team rebuilds the workbook from the last person who touched it.

D. It depends on the tenant.

The strongest process is not the one with the longest explanation.

It is the one that makes the next step obvious.

For CAM, that means source files, lease rules, calculation workbooks, and tenant-facing support are already connected before the request arrives.

Which answer is closest to the real workflow?

For MRI CAM review, three files carry much of the load:

Recovery Reconciliation.
GL Transaction Detail.
Rent roll.

The first shows the tenant recovery result.

The second proves what fed the expense pool.

The third gives the tenant roster, rentable SF, and timing.

If tenant IDs or suites are missing, matching turns fragile fast.

If the GL is summary-level, classification gets harder than it needs to be.

If the entity is wrong, the rest of the review is noise.

Export QA is not admin work. It is the control that decides whether the math review starts on solid ground.

A cap can be applied to the right expenses and still drift.

One common source is the compounding base.

If the lease says the cap grows from the prior cap ceiling, but the workbook grows it from the prior billed amount, the ceiling can fall behind year after year.

That error may stay hidden while actuals are below the cap.

It shows up when expenses spike and the ceiling finally matters.

The check:

Find the base year.
Find the allowed annual increase.
Find the prior ceiling.
Recalculate the current ceiling from the lease rule.

Do that before debating the variance.

Carousel outline: Gross-up review in the right order

Slide 1: Gross-up is not one number
- It is a lease rule plus an expense classification.

Slide 2: Start with the clause
- Does the lease permit gross-up, and what target does it define?

Slide 3: Confirm actual occupancy
- Use the period and measurement basis the lease requires.

Slide 4: Split the pool
- Fixed costs stay fixed. Variable costs are the gross-up candidates.

Slide 5: Apply the target
- Variable expenses divided by actual occupancy, multiplied by target occupancy.

Slide 6: Add fixed costs back
- Do not gross up the whole operating pool.

Slide 7: Keep the workbook
- Occupancy, target, classifications, and final pool need to be retrievable.

Slide 8: The control
- The formula is simple. The evidence around it is the work.

Before a BOMA 2024 measurement update reaches billing, run it twice.

Once with the current measurements.

Once with the updated measurements.

Then compare tenant by tenant.

The point is not to turn a measurement standard into a dispute.

The point is to know what changed before a statement goes out.

Useful backup includes the old rentable SF, new rentable SF, denominator movement, pro-rata impact, and the lease language that controls whether the update applies now.

No surprise measurement changes.

No mystery denominator.

No certification claim needed.

Admin fee circularity is easy to miss because the rate looks right.

The problem is the base.

If the lease defines the fee as a percentage of total CAM expenses and total CAM includes the fee, the fee depends on a number that includes itself.

That needs an explicit method.

Otherwise the spreadsheet may quietly do something else:

Calculate on the pool before the fee.
Calculate on the pool after the fee.
Stop after one pass.
Apply a cap late.

Same rate. Different answer.

The backup should show the method, not just the percentage.

"The system calculated it" is not enough support for CAM.

The system still needs instructions.

Gross-up threshold.
Expense exclusions.
Cap type.
Denominator.
Admin fee method.
Partial-year treatment.

Those are lease rules before they are software settings.

CapVeri's export-first approach keeps the ERP as the source system and runs a traceable calculation layer beside it.

That matters because a reconciliation question rarely starts with "which button was clicked?"

It starts with "why did this tenant get this number?"

The answer needs a source file, a lease rule, and math that can be rerun.

Carousel outline: The pro-rata share check

Slide 1: The percentage is not the whole story
- A clean-looking share can still use the wrong denominator.

Slide 2: Confirm the numerator
- Tenant rentable SF from the lease abstract or controlling measurement source.

Slide 3: Confirm the denominator
- Building leasable area, or the lease-defined denominator.

Slide 4: Watch leased area
- Vacant space should not disappear unless the lease says the method allows it.

Slide 5: Watch excluded anchors
- If anchors are excluded, the effective denominator changes for inline tenants.

Slide 6: Watch remeasurement
- BOMA updates can move RSF and pro-rata shares when the lease permits it.

Slide 7: Watch partial-year changes
- Expansions, contractions, move-ins, and move-outs need date ranges.

Slide 8: Keep the schedule
- The tenant percentage needs a source, not just a cell value.

A spreadsheet can look like data and still behave like a report.

Yardi exports often carry report furniture:

Title rows.
Header bands.
Subtotal rows.
Page totals.
Footer notes.

Those are readable for humans and painful for validation.

Before the CAM file goes into any review process, flatten it.

One row per record.
Column names in one header row.
No hidden totals mixed into transaction data.

This is not cosmetic.

It decides whether the file can be tied, filtered, and traced without accidental double-counting.

The first week after a CAM audit request should not be spent asking where the documents are.

It should be spent checking that the packet matches the reconciliation that was sent.

That means:

Final GL export.
Invoice index.
Management fee backup.
Pro-rata schedule.
Gross-up workbook.
Cap schedule.
Tax and insurance support.
Lease amendment register.

The packet does not need drama.

It needs version control.

If the team has to recreate the support on demand, each manual step creates another place for the story to change.

A recovery gap without reason codes is just a number.

Useful reason codes are specific:

Unmapped GL account.
Lease-excluded category.
Cap limitation.
Gross-up not applied.
Vacancy absorption.
Tenant setup issue.
Estimate billing shortfall.

That list turns a portfolio-level gap into work the team can assign.

Some items may be recoverable.

Some may be permanently excluded.

Some may point to setup controls for next year.

The important part is not pretending the gap is one thing.

It rarely is.

Carousel outline: Cumulative cap bank review

Slide 1: A cap bank is not a note
- It is a year-by-year schedule.

Slide 2: Confirm the lease type
- Cumulative and non-cumulative caps behave differently.

Slide 3: Start with the base
- Base year controllable amount and tenant share.

Slide 4: Build the ceiling
- Apply the annual cap percentage to the correct prior ceiling.

Slide 5: Compare actuals
- Actual controllable amount versus allowed ceiling.

Slide 6: Track unused capacity
- If cumulative, bank unused capacity for later years.

Slide 7: Track draws
- When actuals exceed the base ceiling, show the bank draw.

Slide 8: Keep it portable
- The schedule should survive a sale, staff change, or audit request.

An estimate letter should have backup before it has a PDF.

At minimum, the file should answer:

What prior-year actuals were used?
What vendor changes were assumed?
What inflation or rate movement was applied?
What tenant share was used?
What monthly amount was billed?
What changed during the year?

That does not make the estimate perfect.

It makes the estimate explainable when the year-end reconciliation lands.

The worst time to document the estimate logic is after the tenant asks why the true-up moved.

AI is useful when the file is messy.

Lease PDFs are messy.
GL descriptions are messy.
Amendments are messy.
Expense categories are messy.

That is a reading problem.

The charge calculation is different.

Once the clause, category, date, and amount are extracted, the next question is whether a reviewer can confirm the inputs and rerun the formula.

AI can help with the first read.

It should not be the final authority on what a tenant owes.

A tenant asks one narrow question:

"Why did our management fee increase?"

The answer should not require opening five old workbooks.

The clean file has:

The lease clause.
The fee method.
The expense base.
The cap treatment.
The calculation.
The prior-year comparison.

That is the difference between a response and a search project.

Which CAM question takes the longest for teams to answer today?

Gross-up, management fee, cap, denominator, or estimate billing?

CAM reconciliation gets easier to defend when the answer is built from the same pieces every time.

Source export.
Lease rule.
Calculation input.
Deterministic math.
Reviewer note.
Tenant-facing support.

That sequence is not flashy.

It is the part that keeps the file usable after the close, after the staff change, and after the tenant question.

CapVeri is built for that kind of review:

Export-based inputs, traceable calculations, and backup a property team can actually hand over.

What would make your next reconciliation file easier to defend?

The useful Yardi export question is not "did the report run?"

It is:

What did the export force the team to exclude, fix, or rerun?

A clean CAM review should leave an exception queue:

Missing tenant names.
Summary output where detail was needed.
Recovery pools with no GL support.
Rent roll rows without rentable SF.
Date filters that do not match the close period.
Excel report rows mixed into transaction data.

Those are not spreadsheet annoyances.

They are the points where a later tenant question will ask for support the file cannot provide.

CapVeri's export-first workflow treats those exceptions as the first review, before gross-up, caps, or pro-rata math get attention.

Gross-up support should show more than the final adjusted pool.

It should show the threshold ledger.

Actual occupancy.
Lease target.
Variable expense pool.
Fixed expense pool.
Gross-up factor.
Adjusted variable expense.
Fixed costs added back unchanged.

That order matters.

If the file cannot show which costs stayed fixed, the tenant or reviewer has to infer the treatment from the final number.

That is a weak place to stand.

The calculation is not hard. The hard part is leaving enough evidence that the team can prove the right costs entered the formula.

Carousel outline: The first CAM documentation response packet

Slide 1: Do not start with every invoice
- Start with the records that explain the reconciliation.

Slide 2: Reconciliation statement
- The exact statement sent to the tenant.

Slide 3: Calculation workbook
- Expense pools, pro-rata shares, gross-up, caps, and estimate credits.

Slide 4: GL detail
- Recoverable accounts for the audit year, with account, vendor, date, and amount.

Slide 5: Rent roll
- Tenant, suite, square footage, lease dates, and share percentage.

Slide 6: Tax and insurance support
- Bills, assessments, declarations, or summary backup tied to the year.

Slide 7: Redaction check
- Remove other tenant terms, payment history, and internal communications.

Slide 8: The control
- Send enough structure for review without turning the first response into a data dump.

MRI Tenant Billing History is not always the first file to pull.

But when the question is "what did we bill during the year?" it matters.

Recovery Reconciliation can show the recovery result.

GL Transaction Detail can show what hit the expense pool.

The rent roll can show who was in the building and what square footage applied.

Tenant Billing History answers a different question:

Which estimates were actually invoiced, and did a mid-year estimate change reach the tenant?

That is the difference between checking spend and checking collection.

Both sides of the reconciliation need support.

One building can have more than one CAM denominator.

That is where copy-paste math gets dangerous.

One lease may reference total rentable area.
Another may reference gross leasable area.
Another may have an occupied-area floor.
Another may freeze a measurement standard from an older lease form.

The control is a denominator ledger by tenant:

Lease clause.
Interpreted denominator.
Square footage source.
Current value.
Prior-year value.
Reason for any change.

Then each tenant share is calculated from its own rule.

The portfolio view comes after that, with a total recovery check to make sure the allocations do not exceed the recoverable pool.

Cumulative CAM caps are fragile during handoffs.

The number that matters is not only this year's cap ceiling.

It is the unused capacity carried from prior years, if the lease allows banking.

When a property changes ownership or the accounting seat turns over, that bank can disappear into old spreadsheets.

A useful handoff file should include:

Lease language for cap type.
Base amount.
Annual cap percentage.
Actual controllable expenses by year.
Amount billed by year.
Bank balance by year.
Expiration or renewal notes.

If the lease is non-cumulative, say that clearly too.

Silence is how the wrong cap logic survives into the next reconciliation.

Carousel outline: Where admin fee checks usually break

Slide 1: Start with the base
- The percentage matters less if the fee is applied to the wrong number.

Slide 2: Failure point 1
- The fee is calculated from the gross pool when the lease points to a net base.

Slide 3: Failure point 2
- The fee is added twice: once as a GL line, once as a percentage.

Slide 4: Failure point 3
- The cap is missed, or applied to the wrong expense group.

Slide 5: The clause language matters
- "Included in" and "added to" can point to different treatments.

Slide 6: The support file should show
- Base, rate, cap if any, GL treatment, and clause reference.

Slide 7: The reviewer question
- Can the fee be recalculated without guessing what base was used?

Slide 8: The practical takeaway
- Debate the percentage only after the base and cap treatment are clean.

BOMA 2024 does not change the CAM formula by itself.

It changes inputs that the formula may use.

Rentable area.
Load factor.
Amenity allocation.
Outdoor tenant areas.
Building support zones.
Measurement source.

Is the fee calculated on the pool before the fee, or on the pool including the fee?

Rate x base expenses.

Gross method:
Rate x base expenses divided by one minus the rate.

Capped method:
Calculate the fee, then limit it to the lease ceiling.
